III. PROBABLE ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS
A. General Treaty Provisions on Environmental Protection
The proposed Panama Canal Treaty makes special provisions for environmental protection. The two Governments commit themselves to implement the Treaty in ways consistent with protection of the natural environment through consultations and cooperation. A Joint Environmental Commission will review implementation of the Treaty and make recommendations to the two Governments on ways to avoid or mitigate adverse environmental impacts of actions under the Treaty. The two Governments will provide the Commission with full information on Treaty actions which may have significant environmental impacts. This will be done in timely fashion so that Commission studies and recommendations can be considered before the actions are carried out.
B. U.S. Land Water Use Areas
1. Areas for Operation, Maintenance and Sanitation of the Canal
Under the proposed Treaty the United States for the duration of the Treaty will control the land and water areas of the Canal, its approaches, installations and necessary supporting facilities, and in these areas the present rules and regulations on measures for environmental protection in connection with the operation of the Canal will be carried out by the new Panama Canal Commission.
The question of water conservation, deforestation, soil erosion, and water pollution in the Canal watershed are obviously of prime importance as they impact on the effective operation and maintenance of the Canal. Furthermore, since 1974 Madden Lake has been the source of potable water for Panama City.
The Agreement in Implementation of Article III of the proposed Treaty addresses itself to these problems in considerable detail. It authorizes the U.S. to take a variety of measures to ensure that it will have unimpaired use of the waters of the Canal and of Madden, Gatun, and Miraflores Lakes
